[62] THE ROYAL DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE

[63] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period 1999-2002 Recommendation from the Ministry of Defence of 26 February 1998, approved by the Cabinet on the same day

[64] IN A NEW ERA The international community is in a time characterized by profound changes

[65] The development of security arrangements characterized by dialogue, cooperation and community has contributed to improving Norway's security

[66] Nevertheless, many fundamental security policy questions still remain unanswered

[67] These developments present Norway with new challenges in security and defense policy, but also provide new opportunities for participation and influence

[68] However, the main goals of Norwegian security policy remain unchanged

[69] to contribute to stable and peaceful development, protect our national freedom of action and sovereignty, and safeguard our rights and interests

[70] International cooperation is being expanded and intensified in a number of areas

[71] Through mutual and diverse contact, the ties between countries are woven closer

[72] But while these are important contributions to a more peaceful world, it is not enough to guarantee a state's sovereignty and security

[73] To ensure our integrity and freedom of action under all circumstances, the Armed Forces must demonstrate our will and our ability to defend ourselves

[74] Security cannot be created by one state alone

[75] Norway's membership in NATO has been crucial to our security over the past 50 years and remains the central forum for security and defense policy cooperation

[76] This cooperation is based on the distribution of both benefits and burdens, and in today's security situation, more is required for us than just a credible ability to defend our own territory

[77] Active international engagement, significant contributions to NATO's collective defense and participation in peacekeeping operations also outside NATO's borders are an important part of Norwegian security and defense policy

[78] Although on the one hand it is difficult to see any military threat to Norway today, on the other hand it is difficult to overlook the long-term uncertainty about future security policy developments in both our immediate vicinity and in Europe as a whole

[79] Despite the fact that dialogue and cooperation characterize Europe today, the future is unclear and unpredictable

[80] Since an effective and credible defense cannot be built up in a few years, the development of the Armed Forces must not cast doubt on its ability to safeguard our security in the future

[81] A credible defense in a democratic society requires a broad will to defend

[82] Only a deep commitment can ensure both the ability and the will to defend

[83] There has traditionally been broad political consensus on security and defense policy issues in Norway

[84] However, the experiences of previous generations are inexorably pushed further back into the consciousness of the population, and fewer and fewer people have experienced the effects of war themselves

[85] There are far from broadly engaging discussions about security and defense policy in Norway

[86] Can we still take the will to defend for granted

[87] The Armed Forces can contribute to maintaining the will to defend through continuous development and adaptation to new security challenges nationally and internationally, through visibility and presence in all parts of the country, and through conscription

[88] But first and foremost, the will to defend must be based on a unified and comprehensive policy to safeguard Norwegian security

[89] BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES

[90] The previous long-term report for the Armed Forces was presented in January

[91] St. report no

[92] The policy was based on the recommendations from the cross-political “Defense Commission of 1990” (NOU 1992:12), and initiated significant reductions and restructuring of the Armed Forces

[93] Much has been achieved so far, but many large and complicated transformation processes must be continued

[94] The government's security and defense policy is rooted in the political basis for the center-right government that was negotiated at Voksenåsen in the fall

[95] The overall goal of this new long-term report is to create support in the Storting for the main lines of the government's policy

[96] When drafting the long-term report, the ministry has relied in particular on the Chief of Defence's view of the Armed Forces' needs and development, see Appendix 1, and the extensive research work for the report

[97] The Basic Study 96", which was carried out in collaboration with the Norwegian Armed Forces High Command and the Norwegian Defence Research Institute

[98] The Storting has previously asked the government to consider whether the long-term reports for the Armed Forces should be based on a four-year planning cycle instead of a five-year one, cf. Recommendation S no

[99] This report covers a four-year period for the first time

[100] A shortened planning cycle implies increased freedom of action through more frequent adjustments to long-term planning, but also additional work for the Armed Forces, the Ministry and the Storting

[101] However, four-year reports do not mean a shorter time horizon for planning than previously

[102] Defence planning requires a long-term perspective, particularly in view of material investments which often have to be made with a time perspective of perhaps 20-30 years

[103] The report therefore describes the government's long-term guidelines for the development and activities of the Armed Forces, both in the medium-term and in the long term

[104] To achieve long-term goals, policy must be planned in stages

[105] This message focuses specifically on the government's policy during the period

[106] However, the increasing uncertainty makes it difficult to plan in the long term

[107] For a 20-year time period, no one can count on stable framework conditions

[108] The development of the Armed Forces therefore requires that uncertainty be clarified as far as possible, and that planning as well as organization be made flexible

[109] At the same time, the long-term report must provide a sufficiently precise basis for governance so that the main political course can be implemented over time

[117] Chapter 6 describes goals and guidelines for the structure and activities of the Armed Forces, which provide the necessary basis for following up on the report

[118] Together, chapters 3-6 constitute the core of the report, and these parts should therefore be read in context

[122] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period

[123] The regular submission of long-term reports for the Armed Forces reflects the need for long-term planning within this sector

[124] The previous long-term report from 1993 was based on the recommendations from the cross-political "Defense Commission of 1990" and initiated significant reductions and restructuring of the Defense Forces' forces and activities

[125] So far, much has been achieved, but not everything has gone as expected

[126] The new long-term report is anchored in the political basis for the center-right government that was negotiated at Voksenåsen in the fall of 1997, and is based on extensive research work

[127] The report describes the government's political guidelines for the development of the Armed Forces in the period 1999-2002 from a long-term and holistic perspective

[128] The security situation in our immediate area is currently positive

[129] Today's extensive European cooperation will hopefully minimize the risk of future military confrontations in our continent

[130] The Government will work actively towards this, including through military contributions to ensure continued stability in our region and handle crises on a wider international scale

[131] However, security policy developments are uncertain

[132] Therefore, Norwegian security and defense police must

[133] Please also take into account the challenges that may arise in the long term

[134] These challenges include everything from the danger of violation of Norwegian sovereignty to crises and military attacks on Norwegian territory

[135] The challenges to Norwegian security may also include other types of dangers such as the proliferation of nuclear, biological and chemical weapons, terrorist attacks, environmental disasters and international military crises and wars

[136] Norway participates in European, transatlantic and global security organizations

[137] Of these, NATO remains in a special position, but organizations such as the WEU and the OSCE also play an important role in a comprehensive European security picture

[138] Organizations are constantly changing, and thus so are the opportunities for collaboration and influence

[139] Active Norwegian participation, both politically and through our international military engagement, is therefore absolutely necessary to safeguard our national security interests in a broad sense

[140] Further enlargement and cooperation with Russia and other partner countries provide new perspectives for European security

[141] This security is more than ever characterized by interdependence

[142] It is therefore important that the security needs of all countries are met in a predictable manner

[143] There is no military threat to Norway today

[144] Norway's relationship with Russia is characterized by great potential for future cooperation, both bilaterally and within multilateral frameworks

[145] The significant conventional and nuclear military capabilities in the North

[146] However, Western Russia will continue to influence Norwegian security and defense policy

[147] The uncertain political developments in Russia and the possibility of armed conflicts spreading from other regions to our immediate area mean that these capacities may pose a risk

[148] The government therefore places great emphasis on contributing to Russia's integration into broad European cooperation that includes security and defense policy

[149] Norway will continue to depend on political and military NATO cooperation

[150] Due to the changed international situation, the High North is receiving less attention from our allies than before

[151] At the same time, it is expected that Norway, as a rich country, will shoulder its share of the burdens through participation in the joint defense and in international peace operations

[152] Our national defense planning will continue to be based on allied military reinforcements in times of crisis or war

[153] In a situation where NATO is increasingly moving away from earmarked reinforcement forces, it is important to ensure that allied forces can still be deployed in Norway, and that we are able to receive them

[154] The government will place increased emphasis on training and practice with this as its goal

[155] In the long term, there is a certain uncertainty associated with the development of NATO, both as a military alliance and as a political consultation forum

[156] The disappearance of a defined enemy and the gradual increase in member states may in the future make it more difficult to harmonize divergent national interests

[157] To promote our views and interests in the best possible way, a strengthened Norwegian commitment is therefore required both internally within NATO and bilaterally towards our most important allies

[158] The alliance will continue to depend on strong American engagement in European security and defense cooperation

[159] Uncertainty about the American presence and engagement in Europe and the extent of the United States' contribution to the defense of Europe and Norway would be very unfortunate

[160] At the same time, it is important that the European allies are able to take greater responsibility for their own security, and that the European security and defense identity develops within NATO and with American understanding and acceptance

[161] The Government also sees it as important to further develop security and defense policy cooperation with our new alliance members, our Nordic neighbors, the Baltic countries and other European countries

[162] To contribute to continued stability and security

[163] A wide range of measures is required

[164] The armed forces are the cornerstone of the government's security policy and must be able to defend the entire country against military attacks

[165] Main guidelines for the Armed Forces' activities and development in the period 1999-2002 could help to handle crises of varying scope and nature

[166] In peacetime, the Armed Forces must contribute to the assertion of sovereignty and the exercise of authority, including the protection of petroleum activities

[167] Developments in recent years have also increased the need to be able to participate in a broad range of international operations together with our allies, our Nordic neighbors, partner countries and other cooperating countries

[168] The Armed Forces will also continue to be a key instrument for developing cooperation and contact with non-allies and thereby contributing to increased trust and stability

[169] The armed forces must therefore have sufficient capability to meet a number of challenges in peace, crisis and war, both nationally and internationally

[170] Societal, technological and operational basis Our society is gradually becoming more vulnerable

[171] Without sufficient security mechanisms, weaknesses in parts of the social structure can be exploited by individuals, groups or state actors

[172] The government's focus on measures that can reduce this vulnerability will be central to the upcoming long-term plan for civil preparedness

[173] Technological development is characterized by many uncertain factors

[174] Today's weapons systems will gradually improve, but new weapons with revolutionary military significance are not expected in the next five to ten years

[175] A well-adapted military operational concept is a prerequisite for meeting new challenges and applying new technology in the best possible way

[176] The Armed Forces' new operational concept, which is based on the principles of maneuver warfare, has great significance for all of our military activities

[177] Such a way of operating requires, among other things, mobile and flexible forces, the ability to conduct combat at a high pace, the ability to coordinate efforts, and personnel with high competence and training standards at all levels

[178] The business community's deliveries of materiel, goods and services are of crucial importance to the Armed Forces' operations

[179] The expertise and capacity in the Norwegian defense industry are also important for our defense planning, our purchases of defense equipment abroad, and our ability to meet needs that are adapted to Norwegian conditions

[180] In addition, the defense industry provides positive ripple effects for Norwegian society

[181] The Ministry of Defence places great emphasis on ensuring that the Defence's procurement benefits Norwegian industry and technological development

[182] However, the acquisitions must be based on the Armed Forces' needs

[183] An effective and credible defense cannot be built up in a few years

[184] The equipment acquisitions and competence building in the coming four years will constitute cornerstones of the Defence we will have in ten to fifteen years, and will thus be decisive for the government's freedom of action in any crisis situations far into the future

[185] Therefore, defense policy and defense planning must be oriented towards the long term

[186] In the long term, the risk of invasion cannot be ruled out

[187] However, such a comprehensive military attack would hardly be able to encompass more than one part of the country, but could be supported by limited operations against the rest of the country

[188] The government's ambition therefore continues to be to maintain the ability for time-limited invasion defense in one part of the country at a time

[189] Our own resources are not sufficient to maintain a credible invasion defense of Norway over a particularly long period of time

[190] Political and military support from our allies will be crucial

[191] But a surprise military attack must not cause the Armed Forces to collapse immediately in anticipation of allied support

[192] To ensure the necessary national freedom of action, our national defense must therefore have a certain minimum of endurance during a military attack

[193] The ability to defend against invasion in one part of the country does not mean that the rest of the country is left open

[194] The entire country must be able to be monitored and defended against limited attacks, sabotage or terrorist attacks, regardless of whether this is related to an invasion attempt or not

[195] Our defense must also have the ability to assert sovereignty, exercise authority, conduct intelligence, manage crises, and participate in international operations and international cooperation

[196] A nationally balanced defense cannot be maintained without continuing our total defense concept

[197] The principle that society's combined resources can be mobilized for the defense of Norway, if necessary, must remain firm

[198] There is nevertheless a continuing need to further develop total defense in line with changes in our environment and our society

[199] For the first time, the long-term report for the Armed Forces and the long-term plan for civil preparedness are being presented at approximately the same time for

[200] This will contribute to a more holistic development of total defense

[201] If we are to maintain the ability to defend against invasion and at the same time have some ability to defend the entire country against minor attacks, we have too few inhabitants, and the country is too large to transition to a professional defense

[202] Conscription is also important for the Armed Forces' anchoring in the population

[203] Through initial and repeat service, the majority of our male population gains first-hand knowledge of the Armed Forces

[204] Furthermore, military service has an important social and integrative significance in society

[205] The principle of general conscription is therefore firmly established in government policy

[206] But the conscription system must also be assessed and developed regularly

[207] The government sees it as crucial that all able-bodied men continue to be called up for initial service, and that the total service period is as equal in duration as possible

[208] The criteria for serviceability have been adjusted so that more people can be called up for service

[209] Through targeted education, training and practice, it will, in the government's view, be possible to meet most of the future's competence needs with conscripts

[210] Developments nevertheless make it necessary to further develop supplementary schemes to meet special competence needs

[212] Development of the Armed Forces

[213] The security policy situation provides freedom of action to make necessary changes to the Armed Forces' structure and plans in the coming years

[214] The main guidelines for the development of the force structure are: a comprehensive defence where the various parts of the operations and the force structure are carefully coordinated with each other and with the Armed Forces' tasks in peace, crisis and war; freedom of action to be able to meet changing conditions; a sober level of quality and scope of forces to the ability for time-limited defence against invasion in one part of the country and against limited attacks throughout the country is a defining factor for the design of the Army

[215] The army's main contribution to the invasion defense is the 6th Division with divisional troops and three divisional brigades

[216] In order to strengthen invasion defense and contribute to territorial defense, crisis management and sovereignty, the Army will maintain three independent brigades and approximately 20 independent battalion units

[217] Until 2006, 6th Division and one independent brigade will be prioritized in terms of materiel and equipment

[218] Around 2006, the quality of the lowest priority units in the Army may become so marginal that consideration must be given to reducing the number of brigades and restructuring parts of the territorial forces

[219] The Home Guard will continue at its current level

[220] The government plans to prioritize the acquisition of personal equipment in the coming years

[221] The Navy's main contribution to invasion and territorial defense is the ability to secure sea transport and the ability to protect Norwegian territory against seaborne forces

[222] Five minesweepers and four minehunting vessels are almost complete

[223] Preparations for the acquisition of new frigates are underway

[224] It is planned to acquire six such vessels, which will be delivered in the period

[225] Great emphasis is placed on maintaining the current cost framework for the frigate project - if necessary by reducing the number of vessels

[226] A significant capability to combat surface targets at sea will be maintained

[227] Updating of the HAUK class and phasing out of the STORM class missile torpedo boats will be carried out

[228] A new type of missile torpedo boat is being developed through a test vessel

[229] Two KOB-BEN-class submarines are being phased out as soon as possible to save operating costs

[230] A new missile for combating targets at sea is under development

[231] The coastal artillery will be developed and reorganized in a mobile and flexible direction

[232] The Norwegian Armed Forces' ability to perform the coast guard task is planned to be strengthened through updating the NORDKAPP-class coast guard vessels, procuring a new ice-strengthened coast guard vessel and replacing the Coast Guard's helicopters

[233] Air dominance is of great importance to all branches of defense operations in war

[234] In terms of quality, the Air Force will be strengthened through the acquisition of fighter aircraft to replace the phased-out F-5s and lost F-16s

[235] This purchase will be somewhat reduced compared to the current cost framework

[236] At the same time, the long-term need within the combat aircraft sector must be seen in an overall perspective

[237] By 2006, the combat air force will be dimensioned with the aim of maintaining four operational squadrons

[238] It is proposed that the number of air stations set up in war will be reduced

[239] Ground-based air defense is being developed towards a composite mobile and stationary structure

[240] A squadron of maritime surveillance and patrol aircraft, and a squadron of medium-heavy transport aircraft, are maintained

[241] The acquisition of light multi-purpose aircraft is being considered

[242] Two squadrons of transport helicopters and one squadron of rescue helicopters are maintained

[243] In the long term, it may be appropriate to acquire unit helicopters and combat helicopters for the Armed Forces

[244] Compared to the previous long-term report, the government is thus planning, among other things, to purchase fewer combat aircraft, not to acquire new submarines in the next ten-year period and to renew the Army to a lesser extent

[245] This, in isolation, will reduce the Armed Forces' ability to defend against invasion and territorial defense

[246] Nevertheless, the government believes that such a force structure is adapted to current trends and future potential challenges, as far as these can be foreseen today

[247] Our international military engagement must be an integrated part of the Armed Forces' overall activities and structure

[248] Therefore, greater emphasis is being placed on creating a more uniform system for all Norwegian participation in international operations, regardless of the nature of the participation and the operations' organizational framework

[249] Future readiness forces for international operations will be organized as reaction forces, reinforcement forces and follow-up forces, respectively

[250] The bulk of the Army's contribution will in the future be established within the framework of a brigade

[251] The Telemark Battalion is planned as part of this brigade

[252] The Navy and Air Force's contributions will be based on the units currently registered with NATO's response forces and the UN system, but certain additions and adjustments will be considered

[253] A fundamental prerequisite for all efforts is that appropriate contractual arrangements are established that ensure the participation of a sufficient number of personnel

[257] But the development has also created weaknesses related to, among other things, the personnel situation, material investments, training and exercises

[258] Therefore, there is no room for transfers from operations to investments

[264] Development of the Armed Forces Peace Organization

[265] The peace organization shall carry out the Armed Forces' tasks in peacetime, and develop and maintain the Armed Forces' forces

[266] Restructuring the organization will free up resources to implement the overall priorities for the development of the Armed Forces

[267] Cost-effective organizational solutions can lie across defense branches and sectors

[268] Therefore, increased holistic thinking is crucial

[269] To achieve overall savings through organizational measures, it is necessary to view various resources (personnel, materials, property, buildings and facilities) in context

[322] trigger serious conflicts and environmental disasters and have extensive consequences for life and health in our country as well

[324] The military can also be an important contributor to civil society in strengthening environmental preparedness or handling environmental disasters

[325] The defense sector must protect the environment on an equal footing with society at large

[326] Existing environmental problems must be reduced and new problems prevented

[327] The comprehensive action plan for environmental protection in the Armed Forces will be followed up in the years to come

[328] The Government will continue research and development activities on a significant scale to meet the needs of the Norwegian Defence Force

[329] This activity shall support the overall defense planning, selection of operational and technical solutions, and the implementation of the Defense's projects

[330] Personnel policy In light of the increasing personnel turnover in the Defence Forces, the Storting decided on 7 May 1997 that the Ministry of Defence should submit a report to the Storting on the personnel situation in the Defence Forces

[331] The Ministry has chosen to follow up on the Storting's decision through this long-term report

[332] Solving the Armed Forces' tasks in peace, crisis and war places high demands on the personnel's expertise, continuity and experience

[333] At the same time, the Armed Forces must be prepared for competition in an expansive labor market

[334] How well the Armed Forces succeed in attracting, retaining and developing qualified personnel is crucial to the organization's quality and results

[335] These challenges and demands must be met through a comprehensive personnel policy based on a contemporary management philosophy

[336] The overall objective of personnel policy is to have a highly motivated staff with sufficient competence to solve the tasks

[337] The Ministry of Defence is concerned that the Armed Forces do not lose too much competence as a result of employees leaving the organisation

[338] The Ministry will consider a number of measures in both the short and long term to meet this challenge

[339] The armed forces must be made competitive overall by also emphasizing factors other than salary

[340] The Ministry will also take the initiative to develop a targeted recruitment strategy for the Defence

[341] The Ministry of Defence places great emphasis on skills development to meet the increased demands of the future

[342] This must be an integrated part of the business

[343] Family and equality policy measures constitute an important part of personnel policy

[344] The main focus area is measures that help each family move together to new service locations

[345] The Armed Forces must at all times have a personnel structure that is adapted to the organization and operations

[346] Personnel reductions are still necessary, but at a slower pace and scope than previously planned

[347] The main lines of the current policy for the personnel side of the restructuring will be continued

[348] Restructuring under security is a given, and the ministry continues to place great emphasis on constructive and trust-building cooperation with employee organizations

[349] In the current economic upswing, the government's fiscal policy must help to curb growth in demand

[350] The main lines of defense policy must therefore be drawn from a strict economic policy

[351] In order to maintain a credible defense, the current security policy situation does not allow for continued weakened defense budgets

[352] The government assumes that defense planning will be geared towards a real continuation of the current budget level in the first two years of the coming fouryear period and with ½ percent annual real growth in the last two

[353] Together with the reallocations on the operational side, this makes it possible to implement the government's prioritized focus on personnel, materiel, training and exercises

[354] The actual appropriations, however, are determined in the annual budget process

[355] Within our national defense, we are building capacities to be able to participate with military forces in international operations on a limited scale

[356] The development and maintenance of these capacities is an integrated part of the Armed Forces that can be covered within the ordinary defense budget

[357] At the same time, the use of our capabilities in international peacekeeping missions is very difficult to predict

[358] The Government intends that the additional costs of using military capacities in international peacekeeping missions will be financed in addition to, or as a further increase in, the defence budget

[359] The Norwegian Armed Forces are facing two major and absolutely necessary investments to replace old frigates and old/lost fighter aircraft, respectively

[360] Since these two investments must be carried out at approximately the same time, the investment need will be large for a period of time

[361] These projects cannot be implemented by halting all other investment activity in the Armed Forces

[362] Although the bulk of the payments will only come after the next four-year period, the final decisions must be made in the coming years

[363] The government plans to finance part of the costs of acquiring new frigates, or as a further increase in, the defense budget

[364] The Government will continue a national balanced defense that is based on allied cooperation and collaboration, total defense and conscription

[365] The Government's policy will contribute to the development of the Armed Forces towards a long-term goal that is carefully aligned with the tasks

[366] The defense can and will be challenged in the future

[367] A cautious annual emphasis in defense budgets combined with special appropriations and continued restructuring lays the foundation for maintaining a credible defense and preserving the necessary freedom of action throughout the coming decade

[370] INTRODUCTION Security policy basis

[371] This chapter describes the most important framework conditions and challenges for Norwegian security policy at the beginning of a new century

[372] The chapter first provides a brief description of the current security policy situation based on the changes that have occurred since the presentation of the previous long-term report

[373] The main emphasis, however, is on providing an assessment of future developments, challenges and consequences for Norwegian security and defence policy, which will also extend beyond the period

[374] The security policy situation has changed significantly in just a few years

[375] The demise of the former bloc division has eliminated the danger of a comprehensive coordinated attack against Western Europe, but has also weakened the barriers against smaller, armed conflicts

[376] At the same time, developments have opened up completely new opportunities for contact and collaboration across previous dividing lines

[377] Uncertainty is nevertheless a dominant and likely persistent feature of the security policy situation

[378] Security policy objectives Even though there is currently no military threat to Norway, we are still dependent on participating in broad international cooperation to maintain stability and peaceful development in Northern Europe, and to resolve international conflicts and prevent new ones from arising

[379] Within the various security policy cooperation structures, an overarching goal for Norwegian authorities is to safeguard our national interests

[380] The Government will continue its active commitment to achieving this in cooperation with other nations

[381] The overall goals of Norwegian security policy will continue to be

[382] to prevent war and contribute to stability and peaceful development; to protect Norwegian freedom of action against political and military pressure, and to safeguard Norwegian rights and interests; 3.1.2 to secure Norwegian sovereignty; Norway's strategic situation; During the Cold War, Norway was in a vulnerable strategic position in the East-West context

[383] The threat that Soviet submarine forces could cut off supply lines across the Atlantic contributed to a common Allied interest in ensuring a strong Allied defense of Norwegian territory

[384] The defense of Norway was an important element in the defense of Western Europe in a threat picture characterized by the danger of a comprehensive attack along the east-west divide

[385] The political and military situation has now fundamentally changed

[386] The relationship with Russia is characterized by contact and cooperation, while the political situation in the country is uncertain and unpredictable

[387] However, Russia has retained its concentration of strategic and tactical nuclear forces on the Kola

[388] There are also significant conventional forces in this area

[389] The primary task of these forces is to protect Russian territory and secure the strategic forces

[390] Our allies' interest in engagement in the North has also changed

[391] The defense of Norway is not considered, in the same way as before, crucial for the defense of Western Europe

[392] The risk of conflict between Russia and NATO has been greatly reduced, and participation in other potential conflict areas is being prioritized

[393] If unexpected changes were to occur in Russian policy, and a confrontation were to arise again between Russia and the Western countries, it is likely that this would have major consequences for Norway and Northern Europe

[394] It is in this area that Russia borders NATO and the West

[395] Nuclear weapons also appear to play a significantly greater role in Russian defense because conventional forces have been significantly reduced

[396] It has not been that many years since the end of the Cold War

[397] We may only be seeing the beginning of a larger process of change in Western cooperation and in European security policy

[398] Norway's strategic situation will, however, continue to be entirely dependent on the relationship between Russia and the Western countries

[399] Expanded stability and security in the High North. Norway's strategic situation has also been affected by developments in and the enlargement of the EU

[400] With Finnish and Swedish EU membership, the strategic situation in the High North has further changed, even though EU membership does not entail any security guarantee

[401] The EU also has, through its cooperation with other countries and through the process towards further enlargement, a significant influence on democratic development and economic policy in a number of Central and Eastern European countries

[402] Although the conflict potential in Europe has fundamentally changed, and the security situation has improved significantly, the danger of armed conflict has by no means disappeared

[403] The war in the Balkans and a number of other armed conflicts in Europe's neighboring regions show that peace cannot be guaranteed

[404] We have no certainty that ongoing or future regional armed conflicts will not spread

[405] Such spread could also affect our own area, for example in the event of an attack on our petroleum facilities, perhaps primarily to affect our national security

[406] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period

[407] There is also no guarantee that the positive developments in Russia will continue

[408] It is therefore of paramount importance to Norway that NATO remains an effective collective defense alliance that is also capable of assisting member states in a crisis situation and safeguarding their territorial security

[409] Future security policy challenges are discussed in more detail in chapter

[410] Below, the current security policy framework is described based on the changes that have occurred since the submission of the previous long-term report

[411] The status is projected as far as possible in relation to the time of preparation of the report

[412] The military situation in Norwegian areas The military situation in Northwestern Russia The Leningrad Military District in Northwestern Russia, which also borders Norway, forms part of the forward operational area for the defense of Russian territory to the west

[413] In recent years, this military district has also seen a significant reduction in military operations and capacity

[414] From 1993 to 1997, the aircraft force was reduced by about 20 percent, from about 640 aircraft

[415] Within the Northern Fleet, there was a numerical reduction of around 30 percent during the same period, from 210 submarines and larger surface vessels

[416] The largest reductions, however, have been implemented within the land forces

[417] From 1993 to 1997, the ground forces in the Leningrad Military District were reduced by about 60 percent, from 11 divisional units in 1993 to 4 divisional units of motorized infantry

[418] As a result of the general lack of resources on the Russian side, and costly reorganization measures within Russia's armed forces, there is reason to expect further reductions in the total size of the Russian forces

[419] This also applies in Northwest Russia, even though the conventional forces here are relatively better equipped than most other Russian forces

[420] Priority units such as marine infantry and airborne forces also mean that military operability and capacity are better here than in most other Russian regions

[421] There are still a large number of nuclear weapons on Kola, and the submarine-based nuclear weapons of Russia's Northern Fleet are given high priority

[422] The important role of the High North in Russian nuclear weapons strategy means that there will also be significant conventional security forces in the North in the future

[423] The general military situation in Russia is described in more detail in chapter

[424] Defense policy developments in Sweden and Finland During the Cold War, Sweden had a relatively large and modern defense that included one of the largest air forces in Europe

[425] The force structure has subsequently been significantly reduced, and further reductions are planned for the period 1997-2001 within all branches of defence

[426] At the same time, it is planned to increase mobility and flexibility

[427] Reductions in the defense budget of about 10 percent are planned for the period up to

[428] Sweden assumes a long warning period for possible future armed conflicts, and plans are to establish the necessary operational capacity for the war organization within one year of the decision to do so (“re-engagement”

[429] In addition, the Swedish Armed Forces must also plan measures that, if necessary, can increase the existing structure ("growth

[430] Finland does not operate with the same long preparation time as Sweden and has not reduced its military structure and preparedness to the same extent

[431] The Air Force has been significantly strengthened in recent years through the acquisition of modern American F-18 fighter aircraft

[432] Finland maintains its territorial defense through the broadest possible mobilization structure

[433] General conscription will continue within a more differentiated system, but even with a reduction in the war effort, Finland will be able to mobilize a total of 430,000 personnel for all branches of defense

[434] Finland will continue to place great emphasis on its land forces

[435] Greater differences in the quality of the forces are planned, while emphasis is placed on increasing the ability for flexibility and mobility

[436] By 2004, it is therefore planned to establish three brigades that can be quickly set up and used throughout the country

[437] Assertion of sovereignty and exercise of authority Asserting Norwegian sovereignty on Norwegian territory, including territorial defence, as well as Norwegian sovereign rights in maritime areas under Norwegian jurisdiction involves, among other things, supervision, inspection and control in Norway's economic zone, the fisheries protection zone around Svalbard, in the fisheries zone at Jan Mayen and on the Norwegian continental shelf

[438] Norway also has a management responsibility in relation to fishery resources in international waters within the framework of international law

[439] However, regarding enforcement, this can only happen pursuant to international agreement

[440] Enforcing Norwegian jurisdiction in a predictable and effective manner gives credibility to our will and ability to safeguard our rights and obligations as a coastal state

[441] The Government places great emphasis on further developing international cooperation to ensure the best possible management and control of maritime resources

[442] Among other things, the Coast Guard cooperates with a number of other countries' fisheries supervision authorities, including the Russian fisheries supervision in the north

[443] Through the internal coast guard that was established in 1995, the Armed Forces also carry out missions for other government agencies that have tasks in coastal areas

[444] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period

[445] Exports of Norwegian oil and gas to a number of European countries are significant

[446] The recipient countries' dependence on a stable and secure supply, primarily of gas supplies, means that Norwegian production must also be assessed in a European security policy context

[447] This is reinforced by the fact that potential alternative suppliers are characterized by political and military unpredictability

[448] In the short term, this makes recipient countries very vulnerable

[449] In times of crisis and war, it is the Armed Forces' task to protect petroleum installations, both on land and at sea

[450] The plans for this are linked to the general preparedness system for the Armed Forces

[451] In peacetime, the protection and security of the platforms on the continental shelf has so far been a pure police responsibility, while the Armed Forces are responsible for the overwhelming majority of the expertise and resources that can be deployed

[452] In close collaboration with other responsible government bodies, work has been initiated that looks at, among other things, the relationship between formal responsibility, capacity and resource input related to this task

[453] Internal changes in NATO NATO's adaptation After the end of the Cold War, NATO has adapted through revision of the strategic concept, force structure, command structure and, not least, through a sharp reduction in conventional and nuclear forces and military readiness level

[454] The first political adjustment is embodied in the declarations from the London Summit in 1990 and the Rome Summit in 1991, where NATO determined that the threat of a massive attack was no longer present, and invited the Central and Eastern European countries to cooperation and dialogue

[455] Among the many milestones in the almost continuous adaptation process was the Foreign Ministers' meeting in Oslo in June 1992, where NATO decided that it was willing to make forces available for peace operations under a mandate from the CSCE

[456] This was a declaration that was later expanded to also apply to UN mandates

[457] Since the presentation of the previous long-term report, military-political developments in Europe and the transformation of NATO have continued at a rapid pace

[458] At the summit in January 1994, NATO invited a comprehensive political and practical cooperation program with individual states through the establishment of the Partnership for Peace (PfP

[459] The same summit officially stated that, in accordance with the Washington Declaration, the alliance will remain open to new members

[460] This opened up a process that has led to a comprehensive cooperation program between NATO and partner countries through PfP, and at the same time preparation for future membership, including through adaptation to the military structures of NATO countries

[461] Throughout this period, NATO has reduced the scope of its military structure, while its political role has been further strengthened

[462] The ability and willingness to contribute to solving tasks within international crisis management and peacekeeping operations has become an integral part of NATO's political and military sphere of influence

[463] The conflict in the former Yugoslavia and the inability of other organizations to resolve it showed that only NATO had the political decision-making capacity and sufficient military means to intervene effectively

[464] The NATO-led operations

[465] “Force” (IFOR) and “Stabilisation Force” (SFOR) have also shown that NATO can organize a comprehensive military operation outside NATO's primary area of responsibility and in close cooperation with a number of countries outside the alliance, including Russia

[466] Agreement was reached on a new command structure during the defense ministerial meetings in December

[467] The agreement covers the number, type and location of headquarters

[468] The structure will consist of three levels of command: strategic, regional and sub-regional levels

[469] The strategic commands will consist of the Atlantic Command and the European Command, both under continued American leadership

[470] The Atlantic Command will be divided into three regional commands while the European Command will be divided

[471] Norway will be part of the regional command for Northern Europe, with headquarters in Brunssum (Netherlands

[472] The Regional Command for Southern Europe will be headquartered in Naples (Italy

[473] At the sub-regional level in the north, functional headquarters are planned in Northwood (United Kingdom) and Ramstein (Germany), and multifunctional headquarters in Heidelberg (Germany), Karup (Denmark) and Stavanger

[474] In the south, two functional headquarters are planned in Naples (Italy), as well as multifunctional headquarters in Madrid (Spain), Verona (Italy

[475] Larissa (Greece) and Izmir (Turkey

[476] In parallel with this, the so-called Combined

[477] Joint Task Forces Headquarters (CJTF HQ

[478] These are joint headquarters capable of leading mobile and flexible forces that can meet the Alliance's increased need for participation in peacekeeping operations and increased cooperation with partners

[479] These headquarters are also a means of realizing the European security and defense identity

[480] It is planned to establish three CJTF parent headquarters or cores at the two regional headquarters in Europe and at STRIKEFLEET in the Atlantic Command

[481] These will be reinforced and expanded into full-fledged mobile headquarters as needed

[482] The command structure must be adapted to NATO's role in the new era, with emphasis on both Article 5 operations and new tasks related to peacekeeping operations outside the NATO area

[483] This will entail requirements for flexible and mobile forces, expanded cooperation with partner countries, and the development of a European security and defence identity within the alliance

[484] In addition, there are resource considerations - not least St. report no

[486] which also helps to force a leaner and more cost-effective command structure

[487] Economic and material cooperation

[488] The jointly financed budgets in NATO have contributed to the alliance being able to build an effective military and civilian organization and infrastructure

[489] In addition, the programs also have great political value through the solidarity and comprehensive planning shown through joint financing

[490] Significant parts of the military infrastructure in Norway have been financed by NATO

[491] In the period from 1951 to 1996, NATO invested approximately 33 billion 1996 kroner in Norway, while our contribution during the same period was approximately 10 billion kroner

[492] Large parts of the operation of the command structure and other military related organizations have been financed jointly by the member states

[493] At the same time as NATO must solve both traditional and new tasks, the alliance is facing a situation of reduced willingness to pay among member states

[494] Since 1989, the investment program for security has been reduced from approximately NOK 11 billion annually to just over NOK 5 billion, and the requirements for joint financing have been significantly tightened

[495] Jointly financed operations and maintenance through the military budget has been reduced nominally by about 10 percent since 1992, and no compensation has been provided for inflation

[496] As national contributions to NATO's joint budgets have been reduced, national defense budgets have also been cut, but there are significant national variations

[497] To reduce the gap between tasks and resources, extensive reform efforts have been initiated within NATO

[498] However, the savings potential is limited

[499] Norway is an active driver for strengthening materiel cooperation in NATO, primarily through coordination and alignment of procurement and development of new technology

[500] The goal of the established collaboration is, among other things, to achieve savings in the form of cheaper materials and greater specialization

[501] For a small nation like Norway, it is also important to be able to take advantage of existing technology and exchange information at all levels in the development and procurement processes

[502] European Security and Defence Identity For several years, NATO has supported the development of the European Security and Defence Identity (ESDI) and worked to strengthen the role and responsibility of Europeans in the Alliance

[503] The decision from the NATO summit in Berlin in 1996 to develop ESDI within the alliance gave the process a new impetus

[504] Based on WEU's ability to use NATO resources in WEU-led operations, close political and military cooperation has been developed between NATO and WEU

[505] Several key prerequisites for an operational European crisis management capacity are in place

[506] The work of developing a European command line within the Alliance's integrated command structure will continue

[507] However, to give ESDI the necessary operational capacity without establishing new and resource-intensive structures, this must take place within NATO

[508] This will also help ensure the necessary American support for the use of NATO resources in any WEU operations

[509] In recent years, the NATO alliance has been characterized by an almost continuous process of change, both internally and in relations with other countries and organizations

[510] The capability for collective defense has been maintained through reforms of the strategic concept, force structure, command structure and integrated military planning

[511] The relationship with NATO's immediate neighbourhood in Europe has been further developed through the establishment and development of the Partnership for Peace (PfP), the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC), an expanded and formalized cooperation with Russia and Ukraine, and last but not least, concrete preparations for the enlargement of the alliance

[512] These extensive changes have meant that NATO has in many ways strengthened its role as the central security policy actor and the core of the European security structure

[513] The change process is not over, but must be seen as a permanent process to meet ever-new challenges

[514] NATO expansion

[515] NATO's Madrid summit in July 1997 invited Poland

[516] The Czech Republic and Hungary to join NATO

[517] It is planned that actual accession will take place in connection with the alliance's fiftieth anniversary in April

[518] If NATO's security guarantee to the new NATO countries is to be made credible, the military forces in the new member countries must be able to operate together with forces from the other Allied countries

[519] In parallel with the membership negotiations, intensified work is therefore underway to prepare the new NATO countries for their integration into allied structures

[520] Relations between NATO and Russia Russia's opposition to NATO expansion has been very strong and remains unequivocal

[521] At the same time, active Russian participation in European cooperation is of crucial importance for future stability in Europe

[522] There has therefore been broad agreement on NATO's part to develop the best possible cooperation with Russian authorities in parallel with the enlargement process

[523] With the signing of the cooperation document ("The Founding Act on Mutual Relations, Cooperation and Security between NATO and the Russian Federation") in May 1997, a new era began in relations between NATO and Russia

[524] The document provides a basis for an intensification of security policy cooperation and expands the areas for joint consultations

[525] It is in 1997-98 St report no

[526] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period 1999-2002 a permanent Joint Consultative Council (PJC) has been established where NATO countries and Russia can discuss a broad spectrum of issues and, if necessary, take initiatives for joint action

[527] This means that Russia will be involved to a much greater extent than before in the formulation of decisions concerning cooperation with NATO countries

[528] Russia, on the other hand, is not given any kind of authority over internal allied decisions

[529] Similarly, the Consultative Council has no authority over national Russian decisions

[530] The cooperation document also contains a number of commitments of a trust- and security-building nature

[531] These are primarily intended to increase mutual transparency about military activities, including through the establishment of mutual military liaison arrangements

[532] Partnership for Peace and the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council

[533] The vast majority of countries in Europe outside NATO have gradually joined the PfP cooperation

[534] PfP has proven to be suitable because it is based on individual programs that are adapted to each partner country's conditions, wishes and needs for cooperation with NATO

[535] Norway has participated actively within the framework of PfP, including participation in several PfP exercises and exercises “in the spirit of PfP”, both abroad and in Norway

[536] In addition, Norway has held a number of PfP courses for officers from partner countries on various topics

[537] In parallel with the debate on NATO expansion, a need emerged to further strengthen and formalize cooperation with partner countries that are not accepted as members of the alliance in the first round, or do not desire membership

[538] At NATO's ministerial meetings in December 1996, an initiative was therefore taken to establish a Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC) as a new forum for future cooperation between NATO and Partner countries

[539] The EAPC was formally established in May 1997, and the North Atlantic Cooperation Council (NACC) was dissolved at the same time

[540] The established PfP cooperation will be continued as a separate dimension within the EAPC

[541] The main element of the EAPC is a permanent consultation mechanism that has the authority to make decisions regarding the planning, preparation and implementation of joint PfP activities

[542] This gives partner countries a much greater opportunity to participate in the decision-making process for such activities

[543] At the same time, no participating country has the right to block the implementation of joint activities

[544] The EAPC also has no authority over internal decisions within the alliance or the exercise of the alliance's core functions

[545] Broad-based cooperation is planned on the basis of the EAPC Action Programme

[546] An important element of the expanded PfP cooperation is the partner countries' access to establish permanent military liaison functions at allied military headquarters at regional or strategic command level, and on a temporary basis at headquarters at sub-regional level

[547] Bilateral cooperation As a supplement to cooperation within NATO, bilateral relations with our allies have been intensified

[548] With reduced attention to the High North and Norway, it has been necessary and useful to strengthen this part of the overall security policy cooperation

[549] This has led to extensive bilateral meetings, both at political and official levels, as well as greater systematization of bilateral relations

[550] The purpose is threefold

[551] Disseminate knowledge and understanding of Norwegian conditions, secure information about allied viewpoints, and seek support for Norwegian interests

[552] The importance of bilateral contacts for Norway will probably continue to increase in the years to come

[553] This applies not least to our most important European allies who are also members of the EU

[554] Talks are underway with the US, UK, Germany, France and the Netherlands

[555] These are mainly countries that, in a crisis or war situation, will contribute reinforcements to Norway, and that regularly participate in exercises and conduct training on Norwegian territory

[556] The US military capacity still constitutes the bulk of the security guarantee for Norway and the other NATO members

[557] At the same time, the US presence in Europe makes an important contribution to continued stability in our continent

[558] Our bilateral security policy cooperation with the United States is therefore more comprehensive than with any other country in the alliance

[559] Bilateral framework agreements on defense-related cooperation have also been signed with Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary

[560] For these future new NATO members, annual bilateral security and defense policy talks at official level have also been established

[561] It is important to make these countries as familiar as possible with the security and defence policy situation in the High North, while also providing them with information about the situation in Central Europe

[562] The Ministry of Defence currently has 12 bilateral cooperation agreements on defence materiel covering research, development, production and maintenance

[563] Agreements have been signed with the USA, Germany, the UK, Canada, France, Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey, Sweden, Finland and Australia

[564] The agreement with Turkey has been put on hold

[565] Cooperation with the United States and France has been strengthened by the establishment of bilateral working groups that meet regularly to identify programs and projects of mutual interest

[566] The material cooperation also leads to Norwegian products being purchased by our partners

[569] Nordic security policy cooperation Sweden's and Finland's foreign and security policies have changed since the end of the Cold War

[570] Both countries have become much more involved in security policy cooperation in Europe through membership in the EU, observer status in the WEU and partnership agreements with NATO

[571] Nordic cooperation within security and defence policy has also become increasingly comprehensive, while at the same time changing its character

[572] It is therefore natural that the Nordic dimension is given increased importance in Norwegian security and defense policy

[573] Not least, the development of the Nordic defense ministerial meetings has increasingly resulted in a closer and more comprehensive security policy dialogue

[574] Both Sweden and Finland have expanded their involvement through participation in international peace operations, including the NATO-led SFOR force

[575] Nordic cooperation in the former Yugoslavia has contributed to developing the defence policy relationship between the Nordic countries

[576] At the regional level, the joint Nordic military exercise "Nordic Peace" in May 1997, within the framework of PfP, represented a further deepening of defense policy cooperation

[577] Furthermore, the Nordic countries cooperate within the framework of the Nordic Defence Equipment Agreement from 1994, the aim of which is to achieve economic, technical and industrial benefits

[578] The agreement includes coordination of military procurement from both Nordic and other countries, coordination of research and development, production, maintenance and supply of defense equipment in the Nordic region

[579] There is also extensive cooperation between the Nordic countries on support for the three Baltic countries within the defense sector

[582] The system shall include units from all branches of defense, and provide opportunities to merge units in individual cases

[583] The latter may be particularly relevant in connection with management and in areas such as mine clearance and sanitation

[584] The Nordic countries each have relatively little capacity here

[586] Within NORDCAPS, efforts will also be made to develop a capacity from Denmark, Sweden and Norway for rapid deployment, which can also be linked to SHIRBRIG (UN Stand-By Forces

[591] In addition to increased joint Nordic cooperation, bilateral contact with our Nordic neighbors has also been strengthened in recent years within a number of security and defense policy areas

[592] Defence-related cooperation with the Baltic countries Norway's engagement in the Baltic countries has intensified significantly in recent years

[593] From the start in 1994, Norway has participated in the so-called BALTBAT project, which is a collaboration between several Western countries and the Baltic countries on the establishment of a joint Baltic peacekeeping battalion

[594] Norway has had a special responsibility for the training of the Estonian company, EST-COY, in the battalion

[595] In the fall of 1996, ESTCOY trained in Norway, while in the spring of 1997, the company replaced a Norwegian company in NORBATT in Lebanon

[596] Norway has also contributed various materiel to BALTBAT, and the battalion is now considered to be essentially ready for participation in peacekeeping operations

[597] BALTBAT will be upgraded to an infantry battalion with peacekeeping capabilities in the coming years

[598] This means that the battalion must be provided with additional training, exercise and equipment

[599] In this phase, Norway will contribute additional military materiel and training

[600] At the request of the Baltic countries, it was decided in the spring of 1997 to initiate a project to establish a joint Baltic naval squadron, BALTRON, which will primarily conduct mine clearance

[601] BALTRON will partly be composed of naval equipment currently available in the Baltic countries, and partly receive naval equipment from Germany

[602] Norway has taken on a special responsibility for training ship divers, and in this connection will also donate relevant equipment to BALTRON

[603] The American side has taken the initiative to establish a joint Baltic regional air surveillance system to monitor the entire Baltic airspace (BALTNET

[604] The United States has committed to fully financing and leading the implementation of the project's first phase

[605] The next phase will consist of operation and further development of radar facilities and communications systems

[606] Here, Norway has assumed leadership responsibility for coordinating assistance and implementation of the project

[607] An increasing number of countries are providing defense-related support to Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania

[608] To avoid duplication of work and make the best possible use of resources, there has been a need over time for better coordination of this support

[609] As a result of a Norwegian initiative, a forum, the Baltic Security Assistance Group (BALTSEA), has been established, where key defense policy issues related to the Baltic countries are discussed

[610] All supporting countries participate in BALTSEA together with the Baltic countries
