[612] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Norwegian Armed Forces in the period 1999-2002 Russia and the CIS area

[613] Political, social and economic situation In recent years, Russia has undergone an enormous social transformation that has required great costs

[614] Political developments are still uncertain, and the democratization process is by no means clear or complete

[615] Despite some signs of improvement, the economic situation remains weak and unstable, and characterized by public and private poverty and major structural adjustment problems

[616] This causes a number of social problems and challenges for a large part of the population, while social inequality becomes increasingly visible

[617] The Russian Duma has so far had a limited role in Russian politics, both because the presidential power under the constitution is very strong, and because stable party structures have not been established

[618] Relations with the other CIS countries are a central factor in Russian politics

[619] Russia has significant means of exerting influence in the CIS area, for example in the form of military base agreements and through control of deliveries of vital goods such as natural gas and oil

[620] The possibility of exercising comprehensive political influence from the Russian side is, however, weakened by Russia's own political and economic problems, and because development in the CIS states has taken different paths after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, both in an economic and political sense

[621] Today, coordination takes place bilaterally between Russia and other CIS states in economic, military, and political areas

[622] This coordination has a more or less binding nature, and the Union Agreement between Russia and Belarus from April 1997 is the most comprehensive

[623] Security and defense policy factors in Russia After the Cold War, Russia faces a number of new and long-term security challenges, both internally and along the borders with the rest of the former Soviet Union

[624] At the same time, NATO is still perceived by many as a current challenge and a potential risk

[625] Russia's military position

[626] vis-à-vis NATO has been significantly weakened compared to the old Soviet Union, and the Russian defense budget has been sharply reduced in recent years

[627] The armed forces are still characterized by an oversized and fragmented legacy from the Soviet Union, and have major restructuring problems

[628] The implementation of reforms in Russia's defense has so far been hampered by various military sector interests, conservative military thinking from the Soviet period, and in particular by a lack of financial resources

[629] Despite the problems in the reform effort, an overarching goal is to reduce the size of the forces and increase their quality in order to meet new security policy challenges

[630] So far, changes in the armed forces have largely taken place as a result of general trends of decline and disintegration, and not as a result of a set plan

[631] However, it appears that the need for fundamental reforms is increasingly recognized within the military apparatus, not least due to the general economic development in Russian society

[632] This involves a significant change in mentality from the Soviet period, when the defence force's economy was largely shielded from other economic activities

[633] As a consequence of the extensive reduction of conventional forces, strategic nuclear weapons, primarily sea-based, have assumed greater importance in Russian military planning

[634] This is shown, among other things, through the construction of a new generation of Russian strategic submarines that began

[635] The strategic nuclear weapons could have several functions

[636] to maintain Russia's status as a nuclear superpower, to deter NATO and the nuclear-weapon states, to deter new actors with access to weapons of mass destruction, and to compensate for the lack of conventional capacity in the long term

[637] In addition, the START process involves prioritizing sea-based strategic weapons, which on the Russian side are largely concentrated in the High North

[638] The Russian Northern Fleet's main task today is related to the deployment and security of strategic nuclear weapons, and the fleet has limited capacity to perform other tasks in addition

[639] The Northern Fleet will not have the ability to completely cut off supply lines across the Atlantic in the foreseeable future, but will still be able to pose a major threat to maritime activity in the area

[640] Russia has only to a limited extent implemented the unilateral commitments it made in the first half of the 1990s regarding the withdrawal, storage and destruction of its tactical nuclear weapons

[641] The reason is partly financial and technical limitations with regard to destruction, and partly that tactical nuclear weapons still play a significant role in Russian military planning

[642] The emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons has been justified both by the need to compensate for the weakening of conventional forces and to counteract the effects of NATO expansion

[643] Russia's national security concept was approved by President Yeltsin in December

[644] The concept was prepared by the Russian Security Council, and addresses both military and non-military threats to Russia's security

[645] Among other things, challenges related to social and economic inequalities, corruption and ecological imbalance are discussed

[646] It is expected that the concept will form the basis for a new Russian military doctrine

[647] According to the intention, other doctrines will also be developed based on the security concept, including those concerning environmental issues

[648] Bilateral contact and cooperation with Russia

[649] The basis for the further development of security policy cooperation with Russia is linked to two bi-annual reports to the Parliament

[650] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period 1999-2002 terial framework agreements that were signed

[651] One agreement applies to defense-related cooperation in general, while the other agreement applies to defense-related environmental cooperation

[652] In accordance with the former, bilateral action plans for contact and cooperation in the field of defence were prepared in both 1997 and

[653] The aim is to prepare corresponding action plans in the years ahead

[654] The action plans provide for meetings and mutual visits at both the ministerial and military levels, including in the form of annual security and defense policy talks between the Ministry of Defense and the Russian Ministry of Defense

[655] Bilateral defence-related environmental activities are also linked to the action plans

[656] Within the framework of Partnership for Peace (PfP), Russia was invited to participate in the "in the spirit of PfP" exercise "Barents Peace" in Finnmark in 1999 together with key allies, Poland and the Nordic countries

[657] An important prerequisite for greater Russian interest in participating in PfP exercise activities is that the exercises also provide real training benefits, and do not appear as purely symbolic political actions

[658] Contact and cooperation with Russia's border guard forces Russia's armed forces are currently divided into a number of ministries

[659] In addition to the regular forces under the Ministry of Defense, the Border Guard Forces, which are directly subordinate to the President, constitute an important component of the country's armed forces

[660] On the Norwegian side, the Ministry of Defence, together with the Ministry of Justice, has aimed to increase contact with the Russian border guard forces in order to gradually develop practical cooperation related to border control

[661] This has been expressed, among other things, in the implementation of the joint Norwegian-Russian border guard exercise held in the period July-August 1997, where the focus was on procedures for information exchange in connection with surveillance and control activities along the sea and land border

[662] Norwegian participation in other European security policy cooperation

[663] European security cooperation and the EU-WEU relationship were central themes at the EUS Intergovernmental Conference that concluded in Amsterdam in June

[664] During the negotiations, several key EU countries expressed their desire to give the EU a more prominent role in European crisis management

[665] It was agreed to establish closer institutional relations and strengthen practical cooperation between the EU and the WEU

[666] The WEU will continue to be developed as an independent organization, but integration of the WEU into the EU at a later date is not ruled out

[667] The EU countries further agreed to include the WEU «Petersberg tasks», i.e. humanitarian operations, evacuation operations and various forms of peacekeeping operations, in the new EU Treaty

[668] The Norwegian side wishes that WEU be further developed to the greatest extent possible as an independent organization with somewhat equal relations to NATO and the EU

[669] We actively participate in the WEU within the framework of the limitations set by our associate membership, and we have registered both military forces and civilian units with the WEU

[670] However, the increasing cooperation between WEU and NATO has made it necessary to clarify what rights the European allies that are not full members of WEU (Norway, Turkey and Denmark) should have in the planning and implementation of WEU operations that use NATO resources

[671] From a Norwegian perspective, it is necessary that all European allies, regardless of affiliation with WEU, are automatically granted full rights in WEU in all phases of such a WEU operation

[672] The outcome of the WEU ministerial meeting in May 1997 appears to meet Norwegian needs in a good way

[673] Cooperation in the Western European Armaments Group (WEAG) contributes to strengthening the European defense industry and thereby the European security and defense identity, without this going against the transatlantic relations

[674] Through its membership in WEAG, Norway is actively working to establish a multinational body for the coordination of materiel procurement, the so-called European Armaments

[675] By coordinating requirements specifications and purchasing, EAA will help reduce costs

[676] Furthermore, such collaboration will enable the industry to increase production runs and benefit from specialization

[677] In the long term, this could strengthen the competitiveness of the European defense industry

[678] In March 1997, WEAG decided to establish the Western European Armaments Organisation (WEAO

[679] This organization can be seen as a precursor to the EAA, and will take active steps to coordinate research and technology work in Europe

[680] The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) is today the only forum where all 53 European and Central Asian states, as well as the United States and Canada, meet to discuss common security

[681] The organization has undergone major changes

[682] The main tasks today are crisis management in the form of early warning of potential conflicts, conflict prevention, preventive diplomacy, confidence-building measures and democracy building

[683] A comprehensive set of obligations has been developed to contribute to dialogue, openness and transparency

[684] Implementation of commitments regarding human rights, democracy, minority rights and free media are prerequisites for stable development in member countries

[685] The organization thus has a place in the pattern of mutually supportive European and transatlantic security organizations

[686] The OSCE's level of ambition has increased significantly, and traditional crisis management in the form of military peacekeeping operations has been replaced by a more

[687] Parliamentary report no. 22 Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period 1999-2002 ner carried out by the OSCE is conceivable

[688] However, it is most likely that the OSCE will then draw on other organizations with adequate expertise and experience

[689] The OSCE, on the other hand, has missions in a number of conflict areas

[690] These are preventive operations in which diplomatic means are used to prevent the outbreak of conflict

[691] Perhaps the greatest threats to peace and stability in today's Europe are found in domestic political conditions

[692] The creation and development of democratic institutions is therefore important

[693] Norway has been an active supporter in the work to strengthen the OSCE's role in European crisis management

[694] If the organization is to function as intended, it is important that the executive functions are strengthened

[695] This applies especially to the ability to intervene early in a crisis situation

[696] From 1 January 1998, Norway joined the OSCE leadership troika together with the current Polish chairmanship and the outgoing Danish chairmanship

[697] Norway wants the presidency

[698] This will give Norway a very good opportunity to contribute actively to the leadership of European crisis management

[699] Arms control and disarmament The CFE Treaty The CFE Treaty continues to constitute a cornerstone of the European security policy architecture

[700] The agreement is intended to contribute to the reduction of military forces in Europe and thereby lead to stability at a lower level of armaments

[701] It will also create greater trust through openness and transparency in military matters

[702] Since the agreement was signed in 1990, over 58,000 tanks, armored fighting vehicles, artillery units, combat aircraft and combat helicopters have been destroyed

[703] The agreement's global strength ceiling has not only been met, but current stocks are actually below the agreed limits

[704] During the 1996 Supervisory Conference, it was agreed that Russia would be given an additional three years to comply with the agreement provisions in the flank

[705] This means that Russia can maintain its current stockpile of tanks, armoured fighting vehicles and artillery until May

[706] At the same time, Russia received new and larger quotas, so that the reductions to be made up to 31 May 1999 will be far smaller than in the original agreement

[707] The review conference also opened the way for a modernization of the CFE Treaty to adapt it to the new security policy situation

[708] At the same time, there is consensus among the 30 CFE states to maintain the intention of the agreement, and agreement has been reached on the principles for further adaptation work

[709] So far, there is agreement that the division of the agreement area into a NATO part and a Warsaw Pact part will be abandoned in favor of a system based on national force levels

[710] The zones are abolished, with the exception of the flank zone, and replaced by national force levels and territorial force levels

[711] It is proposed that the flank zone limitations be adapted to the concepts in a revised agreement

[712] The national strength levels shall be set equal to the current strength levels after national adjustments

[713] The territorial force levels will consist of national force levels plus a force level for stationed forces

[714] Consequently, each country will have a separate territorial ceiling, which in Norway's case will correspond to our national ceiling, except for a small amount of pre-stocked allied materiel

[715] In addition, the aim is to establish an agreement mechanism that can provide Russia with certain guarantees that no more equipment will be deployed in countries that join NATO in the future

[716] Strategic nuclear weapons In the early 1990s, great progress was achieved in negotiations between the United States and Russia on reductions in strategic nuclear weapons

[717] The START I agreement from July 1991 limited the number of weapons systems to around 13 for each party

[718] This agreement is fulfilled several years ahead of the agreed deadlines

[719] Implementation of the START II agreement from January 1993 will entail a further halving of the number of strategic nuclear weapons in the United States and Russia, to between 3,000 and 3,500 warheads for each party

[720] To a greater extent than START I, the START II agreement is based on reducing the number of warheads rather than means of delivery

[721] In addition, START II prohibits missiles with more than one warhead

[722] While START II was ratified by the US Congress in January 1996, it has not yet been ratified by the Russian Duma

[723] This currently blocks new negotiations on a START III agreement, which could entail a further reduction in strategic weapons

[724] All former Soviet nuclear weapons have been withdrawn from Belarus, Kazakhstan and Ukraine, and these countries have joined the Non-Proliferation Treaty

[725] The Strategic Ballistic Missile Defense (ABM) Treaty was signed by the United States and the Soviet Union

[726] Continued compliance with the agreement will be important for maintaining stability in the strategic relationship between the United States and Russia

[727] In the spring of 1997, agreement was reached that the agreement should remain valid and that it does not prevent the deployment of defense systems against tactical ballistic missiles

[728] However, the technical boundary between strategic and tactical systems has not been finally determined, and here the parties must find politically acceptable solutions

[729] Tactical nuclear weapons have not, in the same way as strategic weapons systems, been the subject of disarmament negotiations

[730] However, both the United States and Russia have imposed political, but not contractual, obligations on far-reaching reductions and withdrawals

[731] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period 1999-2002 of its tactical nuclear weapons

[732] The number of nuclear weapons in European NATO countries has been reduced by 90 percent

[733] The United States has withdrawn all land-based nuclear weapons from Europe, and all sea-based nuclear weapons from surface vessels and tactical submarines

[734] The United Kingdom has abolished its air-based nuclear bombs

[735] The Alliance's nuclear weapons in Europe currently consist of only a limited number of American air-based bombs and a smaller number of British submarine-based missiles

[736] In 1992, Russia, for its part, had withdrawn all former Soviet tactical nuclear weapons from Belarus, Kazakhstan and Ukraine, and has subsequently consolidated land and sea-based weapons in a limited number of warehouses in Russia

[737] However, Russia is still far from the goal of eliminating all land-based tactical weapons

[739] Norwegian participation in international peace operations

[740] A main goal of Norwegian military engagement abroad has been for Norway to be an active and significant contributor to international peace operations

[741] In 1993, the Storting agreed to a proposal to expand the Norwegian UN standby force to 2,022 people

[742] The Storting has also agreed that the Norwegian IRF forces should be able to be used in international peace operations

[743] In the 1990s, at times up to 2,000 Norwegian women and men served in various operations abroad

[744] This increase was largely the result of the involvement in the former Yugoslavia

[745] Since 1996, military engagement abroad has been reduced somewhat, primarily due to the reduced force contribution to the NATO-led operation in Bosnia and the UN operation in Lebanon

[746] Norwegian participation has been concentrated on a couple of major operations

[747] At the same time, Norway has participated in several other peacekeeping operations, including with observers

[748] The efforts in Bosnia and Lebanon continue to constitute the bulk of Norway's involvement in international peace operations

[749] In the fall of 1997, approximately 1,500 Norwegians served in 8 different peacekeeping operations in the former Yugoslavia, the Middle East and Africa

[750] In the wake of the Cold War, significant changes have taken place in international peace operations

[751] These changes are both quantitative and qualitative in nature, and are interrelated

[752] Quantitatively, there has been a marked increase in the number of peace operations, while several actors, including the major nations, have become more active

[753] Qualitatively, important changes have taken place in the operations' overall organization, mandates, tasks and functions

[754] Peacekeeping operations are not carried out by the UN alone to the same extent as in the past, as NATO's involvement in the former Yugoslavia in recent years is an example of

[755] The operations are based on a greater division of labor between various international actors, including humanitarian organizations

[756] This tendency, in 1997-98 where the UN gives the mandate and other actors carry out the operations, will probably become more pronounced in the years to come, not least in situations where the use of military force may be a key instrument

[757] The reason is both the UN's general financial situation and limited ability to lead complicated military operations and changes in relation to the operations' mandate and functions

[758] The decision of NATO countries to allow NATO forces to contribute to international peace operations is significant in this context

[759] NATO's fleet of surveillance aircraft is a very important resource for monitoring and control

[760] NATO also has a command and control apparatus that can direct operations

[761] Norway will be able to quickly contribute with the units that are part of NATO's response forces, which include both forces that are under NATO command in peacetime and forces that are deployed as needed

[762] Norwegian contributions to the response forces include the Telemark Battalion, a squadron of fighter aircraft, maritime patrol aircraft, a frigate, mine-clearing vessels, missile torpedo boats, submarines and supply vessels

[763] Norway regularly participates in two of NATO's standing naval forces, with a frigate in Standing Naval Force Atlantic and with a mine clearance vessel

[764] Naval Force Channel

[765] These forces will be able to be deployed at short notice in joint operations to monitor and control waters and for other tasks according to the mandates given

[766] In general, peace operations have become more extensive and complicated, both because the tasks of the military forces have been changed and expanded, and because of an increasingly close link between military and civilian tasks

[767] The UN operations in Bosnia and Somalia are examples of this

[768] The mandates for these operations have included both peacekeeping and peacemaking elements

[769] At the same time, the military operations are combined with extensive civilian tasks and challenges

[770] This naturally places completely different demands than before on the political superstructure of the operations and the formulation of the mandates, the coordination of military and civilian aspects, and the understanding of the background to the conflicts

[771] Furthermore, greater demands are placed on the design of rules of engagement, the exercise of command and control, the qualifications and equipment of personnel, the intelligence and information basis for operations, and reaction time

[772] Global security After the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the most prominent conflict pattern in international politics changed

[773] One overarching and profound line of conflict was largely replaced by several and more unclear lines of conflict

[774] While the conflicts have increased in number, they have also become more complex

[775] The concept of "international security" contains a number of dimensions that influence each other

[776] Although the risk of major war today is very small, this dimension still constitutes an important aspect of global security due to the major con

[777] St report no. 22 Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period 1999-2002 the consequences that armed conflicts can entail

[778] The non-military aspects of global security include issues such as terrorism, environmental degradation, overexploitation and competition for resources, organized crime, and increasing poverty

[779] These aspects represent major challenges in themselves, but are also important because they can increase the risk of armed conflict

[780] In this connection, the danger of the spread of weapons of mass destruction represents a serious challenge

[781] The end of the Cold War therefore had ambiguous consequences for global security and for the traditional instruments for dealing with security policy challenges

[782] While the end of the conflict between the superpowers laid the foundation for deeper and more effective international cooperation, it also opened up new and more complex challenges, where other issues and actors have come to the fore

[783] This has led to significant restructuring and new, complicated tasks for the organizations that handle international security

[784] Not least, regional conflicts have become a major challenge, placing great demands on instruments and efforts to find lasting solutions to the problems

[785] These developments have brought a number of new challenges for the UN

[786] As new and increasingly complex tasks were added after the Cold War, expectations for what the organization could accomplish also rose

[787] However, the great optimism about the UN's active role has waned

[788] The limitations on which tasks the World Organization can in practice solve alone have become increasingly clear

[789] This has contributed to a stronger focus on the need for reform of the UN organization and on the gap between tasks and resources

[790] If the financial crisis is not resolved, this could have serious consequences for the organization

[791] However, the UN is the only realistic alternative for coordination and cooperation to solve a number of global security policy challenges

[792] In this context, the Security Council has overall responsibility for international peace and security

[793] The Government has worked actively to ensure that the UN is able to solve its tasks in the best possible way in cooperation with various regional organizations, primarily NATO

[794] FUTURE CHALLENGES Europe has historically been characterized by long periods of peace and cooperation, followed by confrontations and devastating wars

[795] Today's extensive efforts to integrate as many countries as possible into the closest possible cooperation will hopefully result in the risk of future military confrontations being minimal

[796] The risk of major war in Europe has been greatly reduced compared to during the Cold War

[797] Norway is not facing any military threat today either

[798] However, Norwegian security and defense policy must take into account the challenges that may arise in the long term

[799] In order to assess future security policy challenges, we must start from the factors we know or see the outlines of today

[800] At the same time, we must take into account the uncertain and unknown

[801] Security policy does not follow any laws or formulas, and the further we attempt to analyze, the more uncertainty must be built into the analysis

[802] Long-term planning must therefore take into account both what is most likely and what will have the greatest consequences

[803] Together, these two factors constitute the risk that planning must take into account

[804] National security has traditionally been linked to the survival of the state as a sovereign and independent entity

[805] Military attacks from other states have therefore been the greatest threat to state security

[806] This is still the case because there is no form of supranational coercive power that can decide and resolve conflicts if one or more states choose to go to war

[807] Equally devastating are civil wars and internal armed conflicts resulting from the collapse of states

[808] However, war on one's own territory is not the only thing that can threaten the collective security of a state's citizens

[809] A number of other challenges will also have an impact on the state's ability to protect the lives, health and welfare of its citizens

[810] This applies to, among other things, weapons of mass destruction, terrorism, overexploitation and competition for resources, organized crime, large refugee flows and environmental disasters

[811] These are challenges where the Armed Forces will be a relevant instrument to varying degrees

[812] But that does not mean that the government considers such challenges irrelevant or insignificant

[813] However, the government's policies in many sectors must be seen in context

[814] Challenges in Norwegian local areas

[815] The military conditions in our immediate areas will continue to guide our own dispositions

[816] At the same time, we must expect that allied interest in and participation in military cooperation specifically related to our areas will decline

[817] In addition to the military factors, which are described in more detail in chapter 3.3.8, other factors will also affect our security policy situation

[818] Regardless of political and military developments, Norway will therefore face a number of future security policy challenges in our immediate vicinity

[819] Assertion of sovereignty and exercise of authority

[820] It is necessary to maintain and further develop the Defence's ability to assert sovereignty and exercise authority

[821] Effective national resource control and management can in itself reduce the risk of conflict

[822] In the longer-term, the Coast Guard, as a result of developments in international maritime law, may be given increased control tasks in connection with fishing on the high seas

[823] The Coast Guard will be renewed in line with the challenges

[824] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period 1999-2002 challenges Norway faces

[825] This means that the Norwegian Defence Force's ability to carry out the coast guard task is strengthened

[826] Further development of the Coast Guard will also contribute to improving safety in civil shipping

[827] Regional resource crises or environmental disasters in other parts of the world may lead to increased pressure on resources in marine areas under Norwegian jurisdiction

[828] Such a development will increase the need for Norwegian monitoring and control work, and for the best possible cooperation with our neighboring states

[829] Svalbard According to the Svalbard Treaty of 9 February 1920, Norway has full and unrestricted sovereignty over Svalbard

[830] The treaty has certain rules on equal treatment between citizens of all contracting parties with regard to important forms of business activity

[831] Norwegian authority in Svalbard is based on the Svalbard Treaty

[832] In 1977, Norway established a 200 nautical mile fishery protection zone around Svalbard

[833] Norwegian regulations regarding resource management have largely been accepted, but it cannot be ruled out that Norway will face challenges in the future in relation to other states in issues regarding resource management in the fishery protection zone and on the continental shelf at Svalbard

[834] Norway as a strategic energy supplier

[835] Security policy developments after the Cold War have meant that the risk of a major war in our region is very small

[836] However, attacks or threats against our petroleum facilities may very well occur in peacetime or in situations of increased international tension

[837] These may be pure terrorist attacks or attacks resulting from the spread of conflicts elsewhere in the world, for example conflicts in which Norway or NATO is directly involved, and where the intention is to exert military pressure on the Norwegian authorities

[838] As the importance of Norwegian gas supplies has increased significantly for a number of countries in Europe, the risk of attacks on the facilities, where the intention is to hit the recipient countries, may also increase

[839] Such estimates can therefore also come as a result of conflicts in which Norway is not initially involved

[840] At the same time, in recent years, a mutual dependence has been created between Norway and the recipient countries linked to Norwegian petroleum activities, as these provide significant and increasing income for Norway

[841] An extensive and prolonged stoppage could have very serious national economic consequences

[842] In order for the Norwegian authorities to retain the necessary political freedom of action, the Armed Forces must have a certain ability to secure the petroleum activities

[843] The scope of this activity and the interdependence that has been created have increased very significantly since the previous comprehensive review of the Armed Forces' capabilities in this field

[844] Some petroleum installations are also located outside the Norwegian continental shelf, and in some cases on the territory of other states, but are nevertheless subject to Norwegian jurisdiction

[845] Cooperation with our allies is necessary to secure petroleum production and deliveries

[846] In this context, there will be a need for further clarification of national and allied responsibilities

[847] NATO is in the process of revising existing plans for the protection of offshore petroleum facilities

[848] Environmental challenges Peace and security are fundamental prerequisites for sustainable development

[849] War can lead to serious environmental destruction, and even military preparations can put a strain on resources and the environment

[850] On the other hand, natural disasters, overexploitation of resources or environmental stress can trigger conflicts that can in turn result in armed conflicts

[851] There are therefore several connections between environmental concerns and military defense

[852] Major environmental disasters in our immediate areas can have extensive consequences for life and health in our country as well

[853] For example, radioactive contamination can affect the food supply both at sea and on land for a long time

[854] Cooperation with other countries' defense authorities can help reduce future environmental threats to Norway

[855] This particularly applies to Russian military radioactive and conventional environmental problems

[856] Environmentally-related cooperation with Russian military authorities also contributes to building trust, both in a bilateral Norwegian-Russian perspective and in a broader international framework

[857] The trilateral environmental cooperation agreement AMEC (Arctic Military Environmental Cooperation) from 1996 between the defense ministries of Norway, Russia and the United States is a good example of this

[858] Defence-related environmental cooperation is relevant as part of increased bilateral contact and cooperation with Russia, but also with other countries in Central and Eastern Europe

[859] It is also important that defense-related environmental cooperation is coordinated with civilian environmental protection authorities both in Norway and in the relevant partner countries

[860] Political and military changes in NATO NATO membership will be a central part of Norwegian security and defense policy for the foreseeable future, and the government assumes that NATO will remain the central security policy actor in Europe

[861] Other organizations, such as the OSCE, the EU and the WEU, can complement this role, but not replace it

[862] In the longer term, however, there is a certain and perhaps increasing degree of uncertainty associated with NATO's development

[863] This uncertainty concerns the development of NATO as a political alliance, potential national contradictions, economics and priorities, increasing specialization, reduced ability to rebuild collective defense and, especially for Norway, a certain risk of marginalization

[864] A challenge for Norway in this respect is its strong dependence on NATO

[865] NATO and Norway

[866] St report no. 22 Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period

[867] Reinforcements from our allies in the event of crisis or war are a cornerstone of Norwegian security and defense policy

[868] To make such reinforcements credible, allied military equipment has been pre-stocked in Norway

[869] If we can meet any military attack in a credible manner, there is also good hope that we can ward off attacks

[870] The military reinforcement concept is therefore important for ensuring continued stability and predictability in our immediate areas

[871] Political and military support from our allies is based both on broad cooperation within NATO bodies, and on bilateral cooperation and bilateral agreements with individual NATO countries

[872] NATO's reinforcement plans and Norway's participation in NATO's military structure are discussed in more detail in chapter

[873] To ensure continued attention to Norway in an allied context, two measures are absolutely necessary

[874] increased efforts to focus on the challenges facing Norway, and active Norwegian engagement in solving the alliance's tasks, not least on the military side

[875] These factors are naturally interrelated

[876] No country can expect solidarity contributions and the promotion of national views and interests without itself contributing to solving common challenges

[877] Norway is considered a rich country

[878] The great emphasis we continue to place on collective defense, on solidarity, and on NATO's guarantee of our own security must also be reflected in our own contributions to the community

[879] Therefore, the possibility of including more Norwegian military contributions to allied mobile reaction forces and reinforcement units, also with new NATO countries as possible areas of operation, is being considered

[880] These assessments must take into account personnel, equipment and financial limitations

[881] The units should be able to contribute to both collectively

[882] defense, crisis management and any NATO operations outside the alliance's primary area of ​​responsibility

[883] Political development of NATO - diverging interests

[884] In recent years, the political aspects of NATO cooperation have gained increased importance

[885] This development will likely continue, and may eventually lead to a change in NATO's fundamental orientation

[886] With the establishment of the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC) and the cooperation agreement between NATO and Russia, NATO has opened up a qualitatively new cooperation with countries outside NATO

[887] This now constitutes a significant part of NATO's activities

[888] In light of this, it will be a challenge in the years to come to maintain both joint defense and military cooperation, as well as the consultation process and political unity

[889] These are mutually reinforcing prerequisites for the strength of NATO cooperation

[890] It is uncertain whether, in the long term, the member states will have converging interests in planning and implementing both traditional and new tasks

[891] Today, the situation in the High North is of little practical interest to most NATO countries, and Russia's future military potential is becoming less and less relevant to military planning in Western Europe

[892] There is relatively broad agreement that political developments in Russia are uncertain, but that is where the agreement ends

[893] It cannot be ruled out that views on Russia will gradually become more differentiated within NATO, and that Norway may become one of the few countries that still places great emphasis on collective defense

[894] Such a development will then place great demands on the formulation and implementation of Norwegian security and defense policy

[895] NATO will probably carry out further rounds of enlargement

[896] When this will happen, and with which countries, is uncertain

[897] Among the strongest applicant countries will probably be Slovenia, Romania and the Baltic states

[898] An expansion with Sweden and Finland would create a completely new situation for Norway

[901] NATO's military structure has also increasingly been given politically motivated tasks

[907] Consultation mechanisms in NATO are being weakened

[914] At the same time, it is necessary for Norway to place increased emphasis on bilateral cooperation with the United States and other key allies to counteract possible marginalization of Norway

[915] Main guidelines for the activities and development of the Armed Forces in the period

[916] NATO's strategic concept is primarily an overarching political-military management document

[917] The document sets out guidelines for the use of the Alliance's military resources and for Allied defense planning, and sets guidelines for the Alliance's other activities

[918] The NATO Summit in Madrid in July 1997 decided that the Alliance should conduct a new review of the Strategic Concept, which was last revised

[919] There is agreement on the guidelines for this work, and the review is to be completed by NATO's next summit in April

[920] Norway will work towards a concise, robust concept that sets clear guidelines and captures key security policy developments

[921] The concept should establish the rationale for the alliance and its activities and must have validity over time

[922] The work is expected to result in a confirmation of core functions such as collective defense and transatlantic connections, while the concept is expected to reflect NATO's adaptation to new security policy environments and new tasks

[923] As a result of strategic and political developments, nuclear weapons have played an increasingly less prominent role in NATO's strategy

[924] The number of nuclear weapons in the alliance has been greatly reduced since the Cold War

[925] Remaining weapons are not targeted at any country, and entire categories of weapons have been withdrawn from Europe

[926] Nevertheless, such weapons still play a crucial war prevention role in NATO's strategy

[927] Their fundamental role is political, namely to preserve peace and prevent all forms of aggression

[928] It is not expected that this principle will change as a result of the upcoming review of the strategic concept

[929] NATO and the European Security and Defence Identity (ESDI

[930] On the European side, a strong political ambition has been expressed to establish a European military capacity within NATO cooperation

[931] This has resulted in separate European command arrangements within the framework of NATO's command structure and cooperation between NATO and the WEU to facilitate the provision of military resources by NATO to the WEU

[932] To a large extent, the framework for establishing a European capacity is in place

[933] The exercise and facilitation of the arrangements agreed upon within the framework of NATO cooperation will, in the years to come, largely depend on support from the United States

[934] As long as the work to establish an independent European military capability is kept within the NATO framework, the United States will probably maintain its support for this work

[935] However, the European allies have been very limited in their ability to follow up on their political ambitions with sufficient resources, which over time may weaken the credibility of the political ambitions

[936] A growing technological gap in 1997-98 between the European allies and the United States contributed to casting further doubt on the possibilities of realizing political ambitions

[937] In the longer term, it is not unlikely that there will be a more prominent European dimension, which could lead to more bilateral European-American cooperation in NATO

[938] The institutional framework for such increased European coordination within NATO will increasingly be constituted by the WEU/EU

[939] This will present Norway with particular challenges as a result of our associate membership in the WEU and our position outside the EU

[941] It would be in Norway's interest to take into account what could become a more prominent European dimension in NATO

[942] It follows from this that Norway should continue to adopt a fundamentally positive attitude towards the development of ESDI and signal this attitude through active participation in further work on these issues

[943] Only through such participation will we have the opportunity to influence processes in those areas where we have legitimate interests to safeguard

[944] The government's assumption is that the development of ESDI continues to take place with American understanding and acceptance

[945] Not least, the crisis in the former Yugoslavia has shown that transatlantic solidarity and cooperation are a crucial prerequisite for crisis management of any magnitude on the European continent

[946] The government therefore assumes that crisis management that directly affects European security must take place with active American participation through NATO

[947] It is also a prerequisite from the Norwegian side that all European allies who wish to contribute to developing a European military capability should have the opportunity to participate in all phases of a European operation, including the planning phase and the political and military leadership of the operation

[948] Therefore, as much of the planning of WEU operations as possible should be left to NATO

[949] All European NATO countries should be represented in those parts of NATO's command structure that may be made available to the WEU

[962] Changing the command structure The work of arriving at a new command structure was as much a political as a military and resource issue

[963] Alliance considerations clashed with strong national interests, and were further complicated by differing views among key allies on Europe's role within the future NATO

[964] A prerequisite for the new command structure to be able to fulfill all its functions was that a correct distribution of headquarters was achieved, both geographically and in terms of type

[965] At the sub-regional (lowest) level in the European Command, there will therefore be both functional headquarters - based on one branch of defense and distributing forces from that branch throughout the region - and multifunctional headquarters based on several branches of defense, without a geographically defined area of responsibility

[966] It was particularly in the distribution of sub-regional headquarters that the member states had difficulty reaching agreement

[967] Here, considerations of common overall needs and national interests related to headquarters on one's own territory met

[968] This made it very difficult to achieve the goal of a leaner and more cost-effective structure

[969] The disagreement over the distribution of headquarters was greatest in the

[970] the inner Mediterranean, which is also the area in Europe where the new risks to the alliance are most noticeable

[972] Poland and the Czech Republic have expressed their desire to join the Northern European Command, while Hungary wants to join the Southern Regional Command

[973] NATO's goal is to start implementing the new structure no later than the summit

[976] will in the future also be dimensioned to meet WEU's needs

[980] During this period, it will be considered whether HQ North should remain an integrated national-NATO headquarters

[982] At the same time, based on our naval reinforcement needs in the north, Norway will continue to place great emphasis on close lines of communication with the Atlantic Command and the United States

[983] Changing force structure NATO's force structure faces many and demanding challenges

[984] It should be able to solve a wide range of tasks from security guarantees to member states via crisis management, cooperation with partner countries and the establishment of ESDI, to new threats and risks, including the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction

[985] The challenge will be to maintain a unified force structure that is capable of handling the full range of tasks

[986] Here flexibility will be a key concept

[987] To address the broad spectrum of tasks, an overall strategy based on a strong element of force projection could provide NATO with the necessary flexibility

[988] Such a strategy will require increased emphasis on force units with high readiness and the ability to quickly deploy to potential conflict areas both within and outside NATO's area of responsibility

[989] This strategy will be based on a long warning period for a broad attack against the alliance, but a short warning period for possible regional attacks against NATO countries, or situations where regional crises or conflicts on NATO's periphery could spread to NATO countries

[990] Maintaining the ability to rebuild within the framework of longer notice periods will then become a key challenge

[991] A force structure based on such a concept would be able to embrace both the security guarantee towards NATO countries as well as the challenge inherent in crisis management and the possibility of NATO becoming increasingly involved militarily outside NATO's primary area of ​​responsibility

[992] In line with this development, most NATO countries are constantly reducing their military capacity and readiness

[993] Ambitions are increasingly directed towards being able to participate with emergency forces in non-Article 5 operations, and the scope and frequency of traditional allied exercises on Norwegian territory are decreasing

[994] If NATO or the largest contributors to NATO are engaged in a major regional conflict, the alliance will have limited resources to deploy quickly in a possible new conflict

[995] The shortage will mainly be in lifting capacity, support functions and logistics, not the number of soldiers

[996] This suggests that we cannot and should not count on allied support to make up for any weakness and deficiency in our own defense

[997] In Europe, attention among our allies will increasingly be focused on developments in the southern region and in new member states

[998] We must therefore expect that the scope and frequency of allied exercises on Norwegian territory will be reduced

[999] This will have consequences for both allies and the effectiveness and credibility of Norwegian forces

[1000] It will therefore be a major challenge for Norway to maintain Allied interest in the High North, and to create conditions for continued Allied exercises and training at an adequate level on Norwegian territory

[1001] There are major differences among member states in their focus on research and material investments

[1002] There are also tendencies towards a growing technological gap between the United States and the rest of the alliance, which over time could affect the ability of European forces to operate together with American forces

[1003] As the demands for specialized technological expertise increase, this could also lead to a distinction between countries with professional forces and countries that rely on conscription defense

[1004] A growing technological gap and national specialization could thus weaken integrated military cooperation if different countries emphasize different aspects of NATO cooperation and become less willing or able to participate in all NATO tasks

[1253] Future disarmament

[1254] It is a goal of the government to contribute to continued balanced, conventional arms control in Europe

[1255] Norway is among the countries that have the most to gain from the CFE Treaty remaining a central and stabilizing instrument in Europe in the future

[1256] Negotiations on an adaptation of the CFE Agreement are therefore given high priority on the Norwegian side

[1257] There are many indications that the new and adapted CFE agreement will differ significantly from the agreement we have today

[1258] The division of the agreement area into an eastern and a western part will be replaced by a system based on national ceilings

[1259] In addition, there will be a separate ceiling for stationed forces

[1260] Zoning will be abolished with the exception of the flank zone

[1261] In the Norwegian government's view, it is a prerequisite for future stability that Russia continues to be divided into territories with its own material ceilings, that is, that the flank zone is maintained

[1262] Most countries no longer see a need for such large quantities of treaty-regulated material as when the agreement was signed

[1263] Therefore, the collective power ceilings will probably be reduced

[1264] NATO will likely make a cut in its material ceilings by 10-15 percent

[1265] Norway received low strength ceilings in 1990 and will therefore not make any reductions in its own ceilings

[1266] There is much evidence that a renegotiated CFE agreement will continue to be important in limiting Russia's ability to deploy and concentrate forces on its own territory

[1267] For Norway, this is of central importance

[1306] Main guidelines for Norwegian engagement

[1307] Participation in international peace operations is an integral part of the work to achieve international peace and stability

[1353] Weapons of mass destruction and the risk of proliferation

[1354] The proliferation of weapons of mass destruction is today considered to constitute one of the greatest potential threats to international stability and security

[1355] These usually include nuclear weapons, chemical and biological weapons, as well as their means of delivery

[1356] General technological development has increasingly made it possible to produce or otherwise acquire such weapons systems

[1357] The effectiveness of international agreements and regimes that regulate or prohibit the production, export and possession of such weapons varies because control mechanisms are often inadequate or non-existent

[1358] Another reason is that some states refuse to join or conform to such regimes

[1359] There are major differences between different categories of weapons of mass destruction in terms of both existing stockpiles and the potential for proliferation

[1360] Today, there is a relatively good overview of the nuclear weapons in the five established nuclear weapons states and in the so-called threshold states

[1361] Fewer countries than previously feared have been able to acquire such weapons

[1362] However, there is no guarantee that states that may wish to build up a nuclear weapons capability in the future will be prevented from doing so

[1363] Although nuclear-weapon states and threshold states are very reluctant to export technology, knowledge or material that can be used to produce nuclear weapons, it cannot be ruled out that such transfers will occur in special situations

[1364] A particular risk factor in this context is the danger of failing control over the large number of nuclear warheads in Russia and weak control mechanisms in Russia's civilian nuclear power industry

[1365] The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1968 is the most important international instrument for stopping the spread of nuclear weapons

[1366] Although the agreement is largely considered to have fulfilled this purpose, it has not been able to prevent a small number of states from initiating and partly implementing national nuclear weapons programs

[1367] The extension of the NPT for an unlimited period of time in 1995 represented an important milestone in the work to achieve global compliance with the agreement

[1368] The agreement is nevertheless controversial among a number of neutral and non-aligned states, where it is criticized for maintaining a privileged status for the nuclear-weapon states

[1369] A particularly important task will therefore be to convince these countries that global compliance with the NPT is in the interest of the entire international community

[1370] While it is unacceptable that the threshold states use the disagreement over the NPT to legitimize their own nuclear weapons programs, it will be of great importance that the nuclear-weapon states demonstrate a real will to disarm

[1371] The signing of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, as well as the comprehensive nuclear weapons reductions by the United States and Russia, thus constitute important contributions to a strengthened international basis for the NPT

[1372] The initiative from Western countries at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva to ban the production of fissile material is a further step in this direction

[1373] Chemical and biological weapons are in most cases technically easier to produce than nuclear weapons and can be developed by states with a limited industrial base

[1374] In addition, the components used in the production of such weapons are also widely used legally in civilian industry and are therefore difficult to control

[1375] This also makes it easier for non-state actors to present and 1997-98 St meld no
